title: From a deleted file to a router in Arkansas: flying in America, 2023 to now
dek: Two nationwide ground stops bracket nearly four years of collisions, blackouts, shutdowns and slipping on-time numbers. The record, what keeps failing, and why one flight in four no longer arrives on time.
body:
On January 11, 2023, every departure in the United States was held because contract workers, trying to fix a synchronization problem, deleted files from the system that sends safety notices to pilots [7][8]. It was the first nationwide halt since September 11, 2001 [26]. On November 13, 2026, every departure was held again, this time because a router installed at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, flooded the Federal Aviation Administration's network with about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds [1].

Between a deleted file and a misbehaving router lie three years and ten months. In that stretch the country had its deadliest air crash in more than two decades, a fatal runway collision at LaGuardia, controllers who lost sight and sound of their planes over Newark, two government shutdowns that reached the airport, and a steady worsening of the plain statistics on whether a flight shows up when it says it will [4][9][11][13]. This is the record, what it has in common, and what the numbers say about flying now.

## The record

### 2023: the warning year

The January stop lasted less than two hours and still disrupted more than 11,000 flights, with more than 1,300 cancelled [7][8]. The transportation secretary then, Pete Buttigieg, told the government to pick up the pace on modernizing the FAA [7].

The rest of the year was about near misses. Seven runway incursions involving commercial aircraft were recorded in January and February alone, the highest rate in five years [22]. In Austin on February 4, a FedEx cargo jet and a Southwest flight cleared for the same runway came within about 100 feet [22]. That August a New York Times investigation counted 46 close calls involving airliners in a single month and tied the rise largely to a shortage of controllers working long hours [22].

### 2024: the audit year

Nothing fell out of the sky, and the figures slipped anyway. Flights stuck on the tarmac for more than three hours rose from 289 to 437 [3]. In September the Government Accountability Office reported that more than three-quarters of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems were unsustainable or potentially so [19]. The warning was specific, public and two years ahead of last Friday.

### 2025: the year it broke in public

On January 29 an Army Black Hawk helicopter and an American Eagle regional jet collided over the Potomac River on approach to Reagan National Airport. All 67 people aboard the two aircraft died [9].

On April 28, controllers in Philadelphia who guide traffic into Newark lost radar and radio for about 90 seconds. Their union said they were “unable to see, hear, or talk to them,” meaning the aircraft in their care [25]. About 16 planes were under their control at that moment [14]. At least five controllers took 45 days of trauma leave, the facility ran short, more than a thousand flights were delayed or cancelled, and United cut 35 daily round trips from its Newark hub [13][14]. On May 9 it happened again [14].

That spring the agency announced what it calls a Brand New Air Traffic Control System, and in July Congress gave it $12.5 billion [19]. In July and again in September, technology failures at Alaska Airlines and then American Airlines each prompted a nationwide stop of that carrier's flights [7].

Then the money ran out. A government shutdown began October 1 and became the longest on record. Roughly 13,000 controllers worked without pay, absences climbed to between 20 and 40 percent, and on November 7 the FAA ordered airlines to cut flights at 40 major airports, starting at 4 percent and reaching 6 before the government reopened [7][15]. Airlines for America counted 5.2 million passengers affected by staffing delays and cancellations during the shutdown [15].

### 2026: the year of the wires

The National Transportation Safety Board closed its Potomac investigation in January. Its probable cause put the FAA first: the agency had placed a helicopter route close to a runway approach path, failed to review it, and failed to act on recommendations to reduce the collision risk [9]. A working group had urged moving that route after a near miss in 2013 [10]. The board's verdict on the crash: “100% preventable” [10].

A second shutdown, limited to the Department of Homeland Security, began in mid-February and left airport screeners unpaid [20]. By March 20, security waits in Houston and Atlanta reached two hours and New Orleans was telling passengers to arrive three hours early [21]. Some airports advised four to five [20].

On March 17 an Alaska Airlines 737 ordered to go around at Newark passed about 300 feet above a FedEx 777 [22]. Five days later, at LaGuardia, an Air Canada Express jet from Montreal with 76 people aboard hit an airport fire truck seconds after landing. Both pilots were killed, in the airport's first fatal crash in 34 years [11]. Investigators found that a runway safety system failed to activate, and that a firefighter heard a controller say “stop, stop, stop” without at first knowing it was meant for him [12][27].

After that the failures were in the cabling. On August 6 a telecommunications fault left the Minneapolis en route center unable to handle traffic for about two hours across nine states [8]. On September 21 a primary circuit to Philadelphia approach control failed, and its backup fiber turned out to have been cut by unrelated construction; no commercial flights landed at Newark from about 9:40 a.m. to 5:20 p.m., and more than 800 flights were cancelled there and in Philadelphia [8].

And on November 13, at 3:54 p.m. Eastern, everything stopped.

::: embed airspace/ | The afternoon of Nov. 13, from recorded aircraft positions: 5,629 tracked aircraft were over the lower 48 when the stop was ordered at 3:54 p.m. Eastern, and 411 at 8:38 p.m. Press play, drag to turn the map, drag the timeline to move the clock.
:::

## What happened on November 13, as now understood

The FAA's account, published Sunday, is more detailed than what officials said on the night. Instability hit 17 of the agency's 22 en route centers and spread to several approach control facilities [1]. The flood of data came from one or both of two places: the radio site in El Dorado, where the contractor L3Harris was installing a new router, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been replaced three weeks earlier [1][2]. L3Harris cut both sites off and the network steadied; as a precaution, about 60 similar routers had the same function disabled [1].

About 3,500 aircraft already in the air landed safely [1]. Operators cancelled 12,462 flights on Friday, 9,082 of them at major airlines, though the agency notes that not every cancellation was caused by the stop [1]. Counting the weekend's recovery, Reuters puts the total above 18,000 [2].

Three details deserve attention.

First, the routers being swapped out were made by Cisco in 2001 and were due for replacement in 2006 [2]. The equipment at the center of what one aviation site ranks as the worst air traffic control failure on record, measured by flights cancelled, was twenty years past its date [8].

Second, the work was done in daylight. Maintenance at major facilities normally happens at night, but this was a remote site and the job was scheduled for a Friday afternoon; the FAA says it will reconsider when such work is done [1].

Third, nobody yet knows why. The agency says the upgrade did not cause the outage and blames the legacy network the new device was plugged into [1]. The maker of the router, Juniper Networks, is owned by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which says the device was “functioning exactly as intended” [2]. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Monday that it is still unclear why this installation set off the failure, and FAA specialists are examining the router at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida [2][24]. The September audit had warned of exactly this hazard: the FAA was running 11,389 separate project schedules with no master plan to coordinate work at shared sites [19].

## What the numbers show

Dramatic days are easy to remember. The ordinary ones are in the Transportation Department's monthly report, and they have been getting worse.

::: chart Share of U.S. airline flights that did not arrive on time
| Late by 15 minutes or more, cancelled or diverted
2023 | 21.7 | 21.7%
2024 | 21.9 | 21.9%
2025 | 23.6 | 23.6%
2026, Jan.–Aug. | 25.3 | 25.3%
note: 100 minus the on-time arrival rate in the Transportation Department's Air Travel Consumer Report: 78.34 percent in 2023, 78.10 in 2024, 76.42 in 2025 and 74.7 for January through August 2026, the latest published. The 2026 figure covers eight months and leaves out the autumn, including Nov. 13.
:::

In 2023 a little more than one flight in five was late, cancelled or diverted [3]. So far this year it is one in four [4]. August, the latest month published, was worse: 71.5 percent on time, with 13,478 flights cancelled, 2 percent of the schedule [4]. The cancellation rate rose from 1.3 percent in 2023 to 1.4 in 2024 and about 1.5 in 2025 [3][5].

The consumer group U.S. PIRG, working from the same federal data, calls 2025 the worst year for on-time arrivals since 2014 and says tarmac delays of more than three hours reached their highest level since the rule limiting them took effect in 2010 [6].

These are not catastrophic numbers. Three flights in four still arrive on time, and commercial flying remains extraordinarily safe by any historical measure. But the direction has been the same for four years running, through two administrations and two transportation secretaries.

## Three things that keep failing

**The wires.** Newark in 2025, Minneapolis and Philadelphia in 2026, and the national network last week were all telecommunications failures, not failures of aircraft, pilots or weather. The FAA's lines run on a network owned and operated by a contractor, and by May the agency had replaced 2,560 of 5,170 aging copper connections [19]. Duffy now wants a new network built by AT&T, Verizon and Lumen, and says he cannot simply cancel the existing one [2].

**The people.** Controller staffing is the thread through the near misses of 2023, the Potomac findings, Newark's trauma leave and the shutdown cuts.

::: chart Certified air traffic controllers: on the job, and what the FAA says it needs
| Controllers
On the job, Sept. 30, 2026 | 11027 | 11,027
FAA target, 2026 plan | 12563 | 12,563
FAA target, as forecast in 2024 | 14633 | 14,633
note: The FAA hired a record 2,235 trainees in fiscal 2026 and reports its highest certified count in a decade. In May it lowered the number it says full staffing requires by about 2,000, citing new scheduling tools. A new hire can take up to two years to certify.
:::

The agency is 1,536 short of its own target, and that target was cut in May from 14,633 to 12,563 [17][18]. Hiring is at a record, and about 4,000 trainees are in the pipeline [17][18]. The gap closed partly because people were hired and partly because the goal moved.

**The money.** Airport screeners have been asked to work unpaid in two shutdowns inside six months, and controllers in one [15][20]. Each time, the result was fewer flights or longer lines within weeks. The modernization program has $12.5 billion; the second phase alone is estimated at about $10.2 billion and has no start date [19]. Duffy is now asking Congress for $50 billion and calling it an emergency [23].

## Meanwhile, at the gate

The government's failures arrived alongside a quieter change in what a ticket buys. In September 2025 the Transportation Department dropped a proposed rule that would have required airlines to pay cash for long delays within their control, leaving compensation to each carrier's policy [28]. Southwest, the last large airline to carry bags free, began charging $35 and $45 for the first two on May 28, 2025, and ended half a century of open seating on January 27 this year [29]. PIRG says bag fees across the industry are $10 to $15 higher per bag than a year ago [6].

So the passenger in 2026 pays more for the bag, has less claim to a refund of time, stands in a longer line when Congress misses a deadline, and has a one-in-four chance of not arriving on time. None of that is dangerous. All of it is why the phrase people reach for is not “unsafe” but something closer to “ridiculous.”

## What each side says

The administration's case is that it inherited a system starved for decades and is the first to fund a replacement. Duffy points to record controller hiring and to the $12.5 billion already approved, and argues that Friday's failure came from the old equipment, not the new [1][18]. 

Critics answer with the calendar. The Potomac collision, Newark, the shutdown cuts, LaGuardia, Philadelphia and the national stop all happened on this administration's watch, and the daylight router swap was scheduled by its FAA [1][8]. Auditors told the department in September that its modernization had no master schedule and no full cost estimate; the department only partly agreed [19]. Democrats in Congress have demanded a full investigation of Friday's failure [16].

Both descriptions are accurate, which is the difficulty. The decay is older than any current official. The decisions about how to repair it, in what order, at what hour and with which contractor are recent.

## What to watch

- **The router.** A finding on whether the Arkansas device was faulty, misconfigured or simply too much for a 2001-era network [2][24].
- **Thanksgiving.** The busiest travel week of the year begins in days, on a network with about 60 routers partly disabled as a precaution [1].
- **The $50 billion.** Whether Congress attaches conditions, such as the master schedule and cost estimate auditors asked for [19][23].
- **The next funding deadline.** Any new lapse would again put controllers or screeners to work without pay [15][20].
- **The monthly report.** September's on-time figures are due this month, and November's, with the ground stop in them, in January [4].

A deleted file in 2023 was treated as a fluke. A router in 2026 is harder to call one. The system that failed on Friday had been described as failing, in writing, by the government's own auditors, and the description was correct.
